```{r setup, include=FALSE}
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
NAVY  <- "#1F3A5F"
RUST  <- "#A64B2A"
GREEN <- "#2E6B4F"

panel_h <- function() {
  v <- tryCatch(as.integer(input$plot_h), error = function(e) NA_integer_)
  if (!is.finite(v) || v < 80) 140L else v
}

# Reserved HTML height: title bar + n panels + gaps. Must match plotlyOutput.
stack_px <- function(n_panels) {
  n <- max(1L, as.integer(n_panels))
  as.integer(80 + n * panel_h() + (n - 1L) * 22)
}

kpss_cv5 <- function(kpss) {
  if (is.null(kpss)) return(NA_real_)
  cv <- kpss@cval
  if (is.matrix(cv)) {
    cn <- colnames(cv)
    if ("5pct" %in% cn) return(as.numeric(cv[1, "5pct"]))
    if (ncol(cv) >= 2) return(as.numeric(cv[1, 2]))
  }
  nm <- names(cv)
  if ("5pct" %in% nm) return(as.numeric(cv[["5pct"]]))
  if (length(cv) >= 2) return(as.numeric(cv[[2]]))
  NA_real_
}

line_panel <- function(x, y, name, col, ylab) {
  plotly::plot_ly(
    x = x, y = y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = col, width = 0.9),
    name = name, showlegend = FALSE,
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}<br>", name, ": %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>")
  ) %>%
    plotly::layout(
      yaxis = list(
        title = list(text = ylab, standoff = 10, font = list(size = 13)),
        automargin = TRUE, zeroline = FALSE, tickfont = list(size = 11)
      ),
      xaxis = list(automargin = TRUE)
    )
}

stack_panels <- function(figs, titles, n_panels, xlab = "Time") {
  n   <- as.integer(n_panels)
  h   <- stack_px(n)
  gap <- min(0.055, 0.22 / n)
  p   <- plotly::subplot(figs, nrows = n, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE,
                         margin = gap)
  usable <- 1 - gap * (n - 1)
  h_each <- usable / n
  anns <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    y_top <- 1 - (i - 1) * (h_each + gap)
    list(
      text = titles[[i]], x = 0.01, y = min(0.995, y_top),
      xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top",
      showarrow = FALSE, yshift = -2,
      font = list(size = 13, color = NAVY)
    )
  })
  p %>%
    plotly::layout(
      annotations = anns,
      height = h, autosize = TRUE,
      margin = list(l = 72, r = 28, t = 28, b = 52, pad = 2),
      hovermode = "x unified",
      xaxis = list(title = xlab, automargin = TRUE)
    ) %>%
    plotly::config(scrollZoom = TRUE, displaylogo = FALSE,
                   modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("lasso2d", "select2d"))
}

plotly_slot <- function(id, n_panels) {
  h <- stack_px(n_panels)
  shiny::div(
    class = "plot-slot",
    style = sprintf(
      "width:100%%;height:%dpx;margin:8px 0 40px 0;overflow:hidden;", h
    ),
    plotly::plotlyOutput(id, height = paste0(h, "px"), width = "100%")
  )
}
```

# 1. Setup and data

This report follows Borah et al. (IEEE Sensors Letters, 2025) in order: missing-value handling, hourly averaging, min-max to $[0,1]$, Haar MODWT, one CatBoost per component, additive reconstruction, then conformal intervals.

Data are the authors' public files ([WaveCatBoost-Time-Series-Model](https://github.com/jborah2/WaveCatBoost-Time-Series-Model)): `CPCB.csv` and `ID1.csv`. Both releases are already hourly (median gap = 1 h). The letter describes 15-minute samples that were then averaged; we use the released hourly files so the numbers stay comparable. AT and RH are plotted in EDA and left out of the models — the letter is univariate.

Sections 1–9 stay on that pipeline. Section 10 holds the extensions (Fourier vs MODWT, other wavelet filters, EMD).

```{r data-glimpse}
cpcb <- raw$CPCB
id1  <- raw$ID1
tibble::tibble(
  sensor           = c("CPCB", "ID1"),
  start            = c(min(cpcb$Datetime), min(id1$Datetime)),
  end              = c(max(cpcb$Datetime), max(id1$Datetime)),
  n                = c(nrow(cpcb), nrow(id1)),
  median_gap_hours = c(sampling_hours(cpcb$Datetime), sampling_hours(id1$Datetime))
)
```

Winter sits higher than monsoon on CPCB PM2.5. That slow swing is what $S_K$ is meant to carry; the spikes on top of it are what $D_1$ sees.

Hour-of-day and day-of-week boxes. A U-shape or commute peaks means a daily period of 24.

```{r eda-boxes, echo=FALSE}
renderPlot({
  s  <- s_re()
  df <- tibble(Datetime = s$times, value = s$y) %>%
    mutate(hour = lubridate::hour(Datetime),
           dow  = lubridate::wday(Datetime, label = TRUE, week_start = 1))
  par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4.8, 4, 1.2))
  boxplot(value ~ hour, data = df, outline = FALSE, xlab = "Hour of day",
          ylab = input$pollutant, main = "Hour of day", col = "#EEF1F5")
  boxplot(value ~ dow, data = df, outline = FALSE, xlab = NULL,
          ylab = input$pollutant, main = "Day of week",   col = "#EEF1F5")
}, height = function() max(420L, round(panel_h() * 2.8)))
```

The 24-hour cycle in the boxes fixes $S = 24$ for snaive, SARIMA, and the MASE denominator. Weekly effects are weaker here, so $S = 168$ is not forced.

## 2.2 Missing values (paper)

The letter's chain is **missing-value handling → hourly averages → min-max**. Negative concentrations are treated as sensor faults and set to NA before filling. Genuine spikes are not clipped.

```{r eda-missing}
missing_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(series, function(s) {
  tibble(sensor = s$sensor, pollutant = s$pollutant,
         n = length(s$y), n_missing_in_file = s$n_missing,
         n_clipped_impossible = s$n_impossible)
}))
missing_tbl
```

The GitHub CPCB file arrives with no NAs. Long identical stretches at the start of July 2022 look pre-filled; we leave them as they are so the series stays the one the letter used. Remaining NAs (mainly ID1) are filled in Section 3.

## 2.3 Stationarity

The letter does not run these tests. They are here so we can say, for the series on the screen, whether a plain AR on $Y_t$ is even a fair baseline.

Two tests, opposite nulls:

- **ADF.** $H_0$: unit root (random walk). A small $p$-value rejects that — the series is not a pure random walk.
- **KPSS** (level). $H_0$: constant mean. If the statistic is larger than the 5% critical value, the mean is moving.

Air quality often fails KPSS and still rejects ADF: not a random walk, but the winter mean is not the monsoon mean. That is the case where Haar MODWT is useful — $S_K$ carries the slow level, $D_k$ the rest — and where SARIMA is allowed a seasonal difference.

```{r eda-adf, echo=FALSE}
renderTable({
  s    <- s_re()
  y    <- s$y
  adf  <- tryCatch(tseries::adf.test(y, alternative = "stationary"), error = function(e) NULL)
  kpss <- tryCatch(urca::ur.kpss(y, type = "mu"), error = function(e) NULL)
  adf_p <- if (is.null(adf)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(adf$p.value)
  kpss_stat <- if (is.null(kpss)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(kpss@teststat)
  kpss_cv  <- kpss_cv5(kpss)
  tibble(
    test        = c("ADF", "KPSS (level)"),
    null        = c("unit root (non-stationary)", "constant mean (stationary)"),
    statistic   = c(if (is.null(adf)) NA else unname(adf$statistic), kpss_stat),
    p_or_5pct_cv = c(adf_p, kpss_cv),
    reject_null_at_5pct = c(
      !is.na(adf_p) && adf_p < 0.05,
      !is.na(kpss_stat) && !is.na(kpss_cv) && kpss_stat > kpss_cv
    )
  )
}, digits = 3)
```

```{r eda-adf-read, echo=FALSE}
renderText({
  s    <- s_re()
  y    <- s$y
  adf  <- tryCatch(tseries::adf.test(y, alternative = "stationary"), error = function(e) NULL)
  kpss <- tryCatch(urca::ur.kpss(y, type = "mu"), error = function(e) NULL)
  adf_p <- if (is.null(adf)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(adf$p.value)
  kpss_stat <- if (is.null(kpss)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(kpss@teststat)
  kpss_cv  <- kpss_cv5(kpss)
  adf_rej  <- !is.na(adf_p) && adf_p < 0.05
  kpss_rej <- !is.na(kpss_stat) && !is.na(kpss_cv) && kpss_stat > kpss_cv
  series_nm <- paste(input$sensor, input$pollutant)
  if (adf_rej && kpss_rej) {
    paste0(series_nm, ": ADF rejects a unit root (p = ", signif(adf_p, 3),
           "), but KPSS rejects a constant mean (stat = ", signif(kpss_stat, 3),
           " > 5% cv ", signif(kpss_cv, 3),
           "). The series is not a random walk, and it is not level-stationary either — winter and monsoon sit at different levels. A plain AR on raw Y(t) is a weak baseline; SARIMA may difference at lag 24; Haar MODWT puts that slow swing in S_K.")
  } else if (!adf_rej && kpss_rej) {
    paste0(series_nm, ": both tests point away from a stable mean (ADF p = ",
           signif(adf_p, 3), "; KPSS stat = ", signif(kpss_stat, 3),
           "). Treat Y(t) as non-stationary. Difference / seasonal difference for ARIMA, or split scales with MODWT.")
  } else if (adf_rej && !kpss_rej) {
    paste0(series_nm, ": ADF rejects a unit root (p = ", signif(adf_p, 3),
           ") and KPSS does not reject a constant mean (stat = ", signif(kpss_stat, 3),
           " vs 5% cv ", signif(kpss_cv, 3),
           "). A short AR on Y(t) is more defensible here, but the daily cycle in the box plots is still there, so snaive and MASE keep S = 24.")
  } else {
    paste0(series_nm, ": ADF p = ", signif(adf_p, 3),
           ", KPSS stat = ", signif(kpss_stat, 3), " vs 5% cv ", signif(kpss_cv, 3),
           ". Neither test is sharp on this window; lean on the time plot and the ACF at lag 24 instead.")
  }
})
```

The ACF peak at lag 24 is the same daily cycle as the box plots. Tree models use lag window $p = 24$ (one day). If the PACF cutoff is much larger, $p = 48$ is also tried on training data only (Section 7).

At $k = 1$ the cloud is tight: the next hour is close to this hour. At $k = 24$ a second, looser line appears — same hour yesterday. That is the lag set CatBoost sees for each $D_k$.

# 3. Preprocessing

Paper order: missing values → hourly averages → min-max to $[0,1]$.

$$
x_{\text{hour}} = \frac{x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4}{4}, \qquad
x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}} \in [0,1].
$$

| Step | What we do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Clip impossible | Negatives and absurd caps → NA | Sensor faults, not spikes |
| Imputation | Seasonal interpolation if any NA remain (`na_seadec`, period 24) | The letter does not name the imputer; the 24 h cycle in Section 2.1 is the natural period |
| Hourly average | Skip — files are already hourly | Released CSVs are pre-aggregated |
| Min-max | **Train split only**, inverted after the forecast | $x_{\min}, x_{\max}$ from train; test never enters the scaler |
| AR / SARIMA / snaive | Fit on original units | Likelihood and the MASE denominator live on the data scale |
| Split | Last $h$ hours = test | Horizons 1 / 7 / 14 / 31 days |

```{r preprocess-demo}
demo <- series[["CPCB_PM2.5"]]
sp   <- chrono_split(demo$y, demo$times, HORIZONS[["7d"]])
sc   <- minmax_fit(sp$y_train)
tibble(
  train_n   = length(sp$y_train),
  test_n    = length(sp$y_test),
  train_min = sc$min,
  train_max = sc$max,
  test_min  = min(sp$y_test),
  test_max  = max(sp$y_test)
)
```

If a test hour falls outside the training range it is clipped to $[0,1]$ on the normalised scale. That is what a deployed scaler would do.

# 4. MODWT (paper: Haar)

## 4.1 Filters and reconstruction

The letter's wavelet filter $p_m$ builds the details; the scaling filter $q_m$ builds the smooth. Haar (the paper choice) is

$$
p = \tfrac12(1,-1), \qquad q = \tfrac12(1,1).
$$

MODWT does not downsample, so every component has length $N$ and the lag $D_{k,t-1}$ lines up with $Y_t$. Depth in the letter is $K = \ln N \approx 9$. The additive MRA used for forecasting is

$$
Y_t = \sum_{k=1}^{K} D_{k,t} + S_{K,t}.
$$

$D_1$ is the fastest band (hour-to-hour changes). $D_K$ is the slowest detail. $S_K$ is the long-term level. Each component is forecast by its own model

$$
\hat D_{k,t} = f_k(D_{k,t-1},\ldots,D_{k,t-p}), \qquad
\hat S_{K,t} = f_S(S_{K,t-1},\ldots,S_{K,t-p}),
$$

and the point forecast is the inverse transform

$$
\hat Y_{N+h} = \mathrm{IMODWT}(\hat D_{1,N+h},\ldots,\hat D_{K,N+h},\hat S_{K,N+h}).
$$

The pyramid wraps the series (periodic boundary). We decompose the **training** window only, so a test hour never enters $D_k$.

## 4.2 Components $D_k$ and $S_K$

Haar is the paper default. The filter menu redraws every $D_1,\ldots,D_K$ and $S_K$ for D4 or LA8 without leaving this section; those families are scored in Section 10. The stack grows with $K$ — use **Graph size** above if a panel is tight, or box-zoom on one band.

```{r modwt-controls, echo=FALSE}
)
```

```{r eda-mra-server, echo=FALSE}
})
output$mra_plot <- renderPlotly({
  s    <- s_re()
  K    <- as.integer(input$mra_K)
  filt <- input$mra_filter
  mra  <- generic_mra(s$y, K, filter = filt)
  lbl  <- c(haar = "Haar (paper)", d4 = "D4", la8 = "LA8")[filt]
  dcols <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(c(RUST, "#C47A3A", "#6B3A1F"))(K)

  figs   <- vector("list", K + 2L)
  titles <- character(K + 2L)
  figs[[1]] <- line_panel(s$times, s$y, "Y(t)", NAVY, "Y(t)")
  titles[1] <- sprintf("%s  —  original Y(t)", lbl)
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    figs[[k + 1L]] <- line_panel(s$times, mra$D[[k]], paste0("D", k),
                                 dcols[k], paste0("D", k))
    titles[k + 1L] <- sprintf("D%d  ·  scale ~ %d–%d h", k, 2^k, 2^(k + 1))
  }
  figs[[K + 2L]] <- line_panel(s$times, mra$S, paste0("S", K), GREEN, paste0("S", K))
  titles[K + 2L] <- sprintf("S%d  ·  smooth / long-term", K)
  stack_panels(figs, titles, n_panels = K + 2L)
})
```

```{r eda-recon, echo=FALSE}
renderText({
  s    <- s_re()
  K    <- as.integer(input$mra_K)
  filt <- input$mra_filter
  mra  <- generic_mra(s$y, K, filter = filt)
  err  <- max(abs(mra_reconstruct(mra) - s$y))
  paste0("Max reconstruction error (", toupper(filt), ", K = ", K, "): ",
         signif(err, 3), "  (MRA is additive, so this should be ~0).")
})
```

A spike in $Y_t$ appears at the same clock time in $D_1$. That is why a lag of $D_1$ is a usable feature, and why the letter can train $f_k$ separately on each band. Modelling uses $K = 5$ (scale $2^5 = 32$ h, one daily cycle) rather than $K = \ln N \approx 9$: extra levels add one CatBoost each and mostly fit leftover noise.

# 5. Models without MODWT

Shared protocol: recursive one-step forecasts out to horizon $h$ (paper Algorithm 1, step 14). Chronological validation inside train (last 14 days) for early stopping.

- **Seasonal naive**, $S=24$: the MASE reference.
- **AR($p$)**: $p$ from the PACF cutoff / grid.
- **SARIMA**: `auto.arima` with period 24, stepwise, small $(p,q,P,Q)$ caps.
- **XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost** on lag-$p$ features. CatBoost uses `boosting_type = "Ordered"` so the gradient at time $t$ does not use the target at $t$. If the CatBoost R binary is missing, this slot falls back to XGBoost.

Gradient boosting (letter notation):

$$
F_M(x) = F_0(x) + \sum_{m=1}^{M} \eta\, T_m(x).
$$

# 6. WaveCatBoost

For each training series: Haar MRA → one model per component → recursive component forecasts → IMODWT / sum.

- **WaveSARIMA**: does MODWT help a linear model?
- **WaveXGB / WaveLGBM**: does MODWT help boosting regardless of Ordered vs default?
- **WaveCatBoost**: the paper method.

All Wave\* models share the same $K$ and $p$ as the non-wave trees, so a MASE gap is from the transform, not from a hidden extra lag.

# 7. Hyperparameters

The letter does not publish `iterations`, depth, $\eta$, or lag $p$. A small expanding-window grid is run once on CPCB PM2.5, 1-day split, using only the training prefix. The winning $(p, \text{depth}, \eta, K)$ are then frozen for every pollutant, sensor, and horizon.

```{r hparams}
if (is.null(hparams)) {
  cat("No results/hparams.rds yet. Run run_experiments.R from the project root.\n")
} else {
  cat(hparams$reason, "\n")
  if (!is.null(hparams$grid_lgb)) {
    knitr::kable(head(hparams$grid_lgb, 8), digits = 3,
                 caption = "LightGBM time-based grid (train only), best first")
  }
  if (!is.null(hparams$grid_wave)) {
    knitr::kable(hparams$grid_wave, digits = 3,
                 caption = "WaveLGBM K grid at the winning lag / depth / eta")
  }
}
```

Starting grid: $p \in \{24,48\}$, depth $\in \{4,6\}$, $\eta \in \{0.05,0.1\}$, 150 boosting rounds with early stopping. Modelling caps $K$ at 5.

# 8. Forecasts and conformal intervals

The letter's conformal score and interval (no Gaussian assumption):

$$
CS_t = \frac{|Y_t - \hat Y_t|}{\hat U_t}, \qquad
PI_t = \hat Y_t \pm CQ_t\,\hat U_t,
$$

with $\hat U_t$ a rolling MAE, $CQ_t$ the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $CS$ on a trailing window of length $\kappa$, and $\alpha = 0.05$. $\kappa$ is chosen from $\{24,168,336\}$ so calibration coverage is closest to 95%. Test actuals are never used to build the band. Lower and upper edges are $L_t = \hat Y_t - CQ_t \hat U_t$ and $U_t = \hat Y_t + CQ_t \hat U_t$.

# 9. Comparison

MASE uses seasonality $S = 24$, matching the letter:

$$
\mathrm{MASE} = \frac{N-S}{h}\,
\frac{\sum_{t=N+1}^{N+h}|\hat Y_t - Y_t|}
     {\sum_{t=S+1}^{N}|Y_t - Y_{t-S}|}.
$$

MAE and RMSE are on original units after inverting min-max.

```{r scores-table}
if (is.null(scores) || !nrow(scores)) {
  cat("No results/scores.rds yet. From the project root run:\n",
      "  Rscript run_experiments.R        # full 6 x 2 x 4 bake-off\n",
      "  Rscript run_experiments.R quick  # 1-day, snaive/sarima/lgb/wavelgb\n")
} else {
  DT::datatable(scores %>% dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(MASE, MAE, RMSE), ~round(., 3))),
                caption = "Cached forecasts (paper pipeline + baselines)",
                options = list(pageLength = 12))
}
```

```{r scores-wide}
if (!is.null(scores) && nrow(scores)) {
  wide <- scores %>%
    dplyr::select(sensor, pollutant, horizon, method, MASE) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = MASE)
  knitr::kable(wide, digits = 3, caption = "MASE (lower is better)")
}
```

WaveCatBoost vs CatBoost is the value of Haar MODWT. WaveXGB vs WaveCatBoost is Ordered boosting after the transform is fixed. SARIMA vs WaveSARIMA asks whether the transform helps a linear model.

```{r mcb}
if (!is.null(scores) && nrow(scores) > 4) {
  mcb <- tryCatch(mcb_from_table(scores), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(mcb)) {
    knitr::kable(mcb, digits = 3,
                 caption = "MCB / Nemenyi mean ranks across pollutant–sensor–horizon cases")
    renderPlot({
      rng <- range(c(mcb$lo, mcb$hi))
      par(mar = c(5, 8, 4, 1.2))
      plot(mcb$mean_rank, seq_len(nrow(mcb)), pch = 16, xlim = rng,
           yaxt = "n", xlab = "Mean rank (lower is better)", ylab = NA,
           main = "MCB-style ranks")
      axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(mcb)), labels = mcb$model, las = 1)
      segments(mcb$lo, seq_len(nrow(mcb)), mcb$hi, seq_len(nrow(mcb)))
      abline(v = min(mcb$mean_rank) + unique(mcb$critical_distance) / 2,
             lty = 2, col = RUST)
    }, height = function() max(420L, round(panel_h() * 2.8)))
  }
}
```

CPCB 7-day MASE values sit on top of each other near 1.50: recursive one-step forecasts have collapsed to “same hour yesterday,” which is why snaive is hard to beat at that horizon.

# 10. Extensions

Three questions that sit outside the letter: why MODWT rather than Fourier; what another decomposition (EMD) looks like; and whether Haar is special among wavelet filters. All three use the same WaveLGB head, the same $K$ and $p$, and the same 1-day split, so a MASE gap is from the transform.

Run `run_extensions.R` if the tables below are empty.

## 10.1 Fourier vs MODWT

Fourier coefficients are global: a spike at hour 1000 contributes to every frequency bin, so there is no $F_{\omega,t}$ to lag. MODWT keeps the time index, so $D_{1,t}$ is the fine-scale event *at time $t$*.

| | Fourier (FFT) | Haar MODWT (letter) |
|---|---|---|
| Time localisation | None — one coefficient per frequency | Yes — $D_{k,t}$ is indexed by $t$ |
| Frequency localisation | Exact bins | Octave bands, level $k$ |
| Stationarity | Mixes winter into summer | Local in time |
| Lag features | Coefficients are not a time series | $D_{k,t-1}$ lines up with $Y_t$ |
| Reconstruction | IFFT | Additive MRA / IMODWT |

```{r fourier-controls, echo=FALSE}
inputPanel(
  sliderInput("fvm_zoom", "Show first N hours", min = 168, max = 720, value = 336, step = 24)
)
```

```{r fourier-vs-modwt-plot, echo=FALSE}
uiOutput("fvm_slot")
```

```{r fourier-vs-modwt-server, echo=FALSE}
output$fvm_slot <- renderUI(plotly_slot("fvm_plot", 4L))
output$fvm_plot <- renderPlotly({
  s  <- s_re()
  y  <- s$y
  n  <- min(as.integer(input$fvm_zoom), length(y))
  ys <- y[seq_len(n)]
  tt <- s$times[seq_len(n)]

  fft_y   <- fft(ys)
  amp     <- Mod(fft_y)
  top_idx <- order(amp, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(11L, n))]
  fft_filt          <- complex(length.out = n)
  fft_filt[top_idx] <- fft_y[top_idx]
  fourier_approx    <- Re(fft(fft_filt, inverse = TRUE)) / n
  mra <- haar_mra(ys, 3L)

  figs <- list(
    line_panel(tt, ys, "Y(t)", NAVY, input$pollutant),
    line_panel(tt, fourier_approx, "Fourier", "#8B0000", "FFT"),
    line_panel(tt, mra$D[[1]], "D1", RUST, "D1"),
    line_panel(tt, mra$S, "S3", GREEN, "S3")
  )
  titles <- c(
    "Original Y(t)",
    "Fourier: top frequencies (no time index)",
    "Haar MODWT D1 (time-local)",
    "Haar MODWT S3 (smooth)"
  )
  stack_panels(figs, titles, n_panels = 4L)
})
```

The Fourier curve is a handful of sinusoids laid over the whole window. Haar $D_1$ is quiet until the event, then jumps. That is the lag-feature argument in one picture.

Same WaveLGB head, Fourier octave bands vs Haar:

```{r fourier-scores}
fs <- ext_scores
if (is.null(fs) || !nrow(fs)) fs <- filter_scores
if (is.null(fs) || !nrow(fs)) {
  cat("No extension scores yet. Run:\n  Rscript run_extensions.R\n")
} else {
  sub <- fs %>%
    dplyr::filter(filter %in% c("haar", "fourier"), horizon == "1d") %>%
    dplyr::select(sensor, pollutant, filter, MASE, MAE, RMSE)
  if (!nrow(sub)) {
    cat("Fourier rows are not in the cache yet. Run run_extensions.R.\n")
  } else {
    knitr::kable(sub, digits = 3,
                 caption = "WaveLGB, 1-day: Haar MODWT vs Fourier bands")
  }
}
```

Haar should win on series with sharp spikes (ID1 in particular). Fourier bands ring around every event, so the lag vector at time $t$ still contains a little of yesterday's spike.

## 10.2 Other wavelet filters (Haar, D4, LA8)

Haar is two taps. D4 (4 taps) and LA8 (8 taps) are smoother octave filters. Reconstruction remains $Y_t = \sum_k D_{k,t} + S_{K,t}$ for every family; what changes is the shape of each $D_k$. Switch the filter in **Section 4.2** to see $D_1,\ldots,D_K$ and $S_K$ for Haar, D4, or LA8. The comparison below is MASE only — same WaveLGB head, same $K$ and $p$.

```{r filter-scores}
fs <- ext_scores
if (is.null(fs) || !nrow(fs)) fs <- filter_scores
if (is.null(fs) || !nrow(fs)) {
  cat("Filter scores not yet computed. Run run_experiments.R or run_extensions.R.\n")
} else {
  sub <- fs %>%
    dplyr::filter(filter %in% c("haar", "d4", "la8")) %>%
    dplyr::select(sensor, pollutant, horizon, filter, MASE, MAE, RMSE)
  fw <- sub %>%
    dplyr::select(sensor, pollutant, horizon, filter, MASE) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = filter, values_from = MASE)
  knitr::kable(fw, digits = 3,
               caption = "WaveLGB MASE by filter family — lower is better")
}
```

```{r filter-scores-plot, echo=FALSE}
if (is.null(fs) || !nrow(fs)) fs <- filter_scores
if (!is.null(fs) && nrow(fs)) {

```

```{r filter-scores-plot-server, echo=FALSE}
  output$filt_slot <- renderUI(plotly_slot("filt_plot", 3L))
  output$filt_plot <- renderPlotly({
    df <- fs_plot %>%
      dplyr::filter(filter %in% c("haar", "d4", "la8")) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        label  = paste(sensor, pollutant, sep = "-"),
        filter = factor(filter, levels = c("haar", "d4", "la8"),
                        labels = c("Haar (paper)", "D4", "LA8"))
      )
    p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = filter, y = MASE, fill = filter)) +
      geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.65) +
      facet_wrap(~ label + horizon, scales = "free_y") +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c("Haar (paper)" = NAVY, "D4" = RUST, "LA8" = GREEN)) +
      labs(x = NULL, y = "MASE", title = "Filter family — WaveLGB", fill = "Filter") +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
            plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = NAVY, size = 14))
    ggplotly(p) %>%
      plotly::layout(height = stack_px(3L), autosize = TRUE,
                     margin = list(l = 56, r = 20, t = 56, b = 40)) %>%
      plotly::config(displaylogo = FALSE)

```

On these series Haar is as good as, or slightly better than, D4 and LA8. The extra taps buy a cleaner $D_k$ plot, not a lower MASE. Haar also matches the letter, so it stays the default.

## 10.3 Empirical Mode Decomposition

EMD does not use a fixed filter bank. It peels off Intrinsic Mode Functions from the data:

$$
Y_t = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{IMF}_k(t) + r(t).
$$

IMF 1 is mapped to $D_1$, IMF 2 to $D_2$, and so on; the residue plus leftover IMFs sit in $S_K$. The same WaveLGB head then forecasts each piece.

```{r emd-demo, echo=FALSE}
uiOutput("emd_slot")
```

```{r emd-demo-server, echo=FALSE}
output$emd_slot <- renderUI(plotly_slot("emd_plot", 5L))
output$emd_plot <- renderPlotly({
  if (!requireNamespace("EMD", quietly = TRUE)) {
    return(plotly::plotly_empty(type = "scatter") %>%
             plotly::layout(title = "Install the EMD package to see this plot.",
                            height = stack_px(5L)))
  }
  s     <- s_re()
  n_emd <- min(500L, length(s$y))
  ys    <- s$y[seq_len(n_emd)]
  tt    <- s$times[seq_len(n_emd)]
  emd_out <- tryCatch(EMD::emd(as.numeric(ys), seq_len(n_emd), boundary = "periodic"),
                      error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(emd_out) || is.null(emd_out$imf) || ncol(emd_out$imf) < 1) {
    return(plotly::plotly_empty(type = "scatter") %>%
             plotly::layout(title = "EMD did not converge on this subseries.",
                            height = stack_px(5L)))
  }
  n_imf <- min(ncol(emd_out$imf), 4L)
  cols  <- c(RUST, GREEN, "#8B0000", "#4B0082")
  figs   <- vector("list", n_imf + 1L)
  titles <- character(n_imf + 1L)
  figs[[1]] <- line_panel(tt, ys, "Y(t)", NAVY, input$pollutant)
  titles[1] <- "Original (first 500 h)"
  for (k in seq_len(n_imf)) {
    figs[[k + 1L]] <- line_panel(tt, emd_out$imf[, k], paste0("IMF", k),
                                 cols[k], paste0("IMF", k))
    titles[k + 1L] <- paste0("IMF", k, "  —  adaptive scale")
  }
  stack_panels(figs, titles, n_panels = n_imf + 1L)
})
```

```{r emd-scores}
fs <- ext_scores
if (!is.null(fs) && nrow(fs) && "emd" %in% fs$filter) {
  sub <- fs %>%
    dplyr::filter(filter %in% c("haar", "emd"), horizon == "1d") %>%
    dplyr::select(sensor, pollutant, filter, MASE, MAE, RMSE)
  knitr::kable(sub, digits = 3,
               caption = "WaveLGB, 1-day: Haar MODWT vs EMD")
} else {
  cat("EMD scores appear after run_extensions.R (CPCB PM2.5, 1-day only).\n")
}
```

| | Haar MODWT (letter) | EMD |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | Fixed Haar bank $p_m, q_m$ | Adaptive IMFs |
| Mode mixing | No — bands are fixed | Possible |
| Reconstruction | Exact MRA | Exact by construction |
| Cost | $O(NK)$ | $O(N^2)$ in the worst case |

EMD can park a dust-storm and a traffic spike in the same IMF if they share a local period. Haar will not: $D_1$ is always the 2–4 h band. That predictability, and the speed, is why the letter's choice stays the operational default.

## 10.4 Air-quality alert (not in the letter)

If the mean of the PM2.5 **lower** bound over the horizon exceeds the WHO 24-hour guide (15 µg/m³) or India NAAQS (60 µg/m³), we flag "exceedance likely." Conservative: even the optimistic end of $PI_t$ is already above the guide.
